248: The fourth Percy Jackson and the Olympians book takes the group into Daedalus's labyrinth as a threat approaches Camp Half-Blood.
249: The Battle of the Labyrinth is my favorite book in my favorite series. Percy Jackson was with me through much of my youth, so I have a strong emotional connection to these books, but this one has always stood above the others for me.
250: It was also one of the works that sparked interests I still have today. My interest in mythology, ancient cultures, folklore and different ways to reinterpret those stories grew largely out of reading Percy Jackson. I can connect this book directly to several hobbies and interests I developed later, so it means much more to me than simply a story I enjoyed.
251: Sherlock Holmes — The Sign of Four
255: The second Sherlock Holmes novel brings together a disappearance, a treasure and a case Mary Morstan brings to Holmes and Watson.
256: The Sign of Four was a gift from my mother, and it was also the first book I remember reading and thinking: "this is a truly complex story." It was one of my first encounters with a more elaborate detective narrative, full of clues, deductions and details that really demanded attention.
257: It left such an impression that this kind of story remains among my favorites today. Much of my taste for Arthur Conan Doyle, Agatha Christie and mystery and detective stories started there. So, beyond really liking the book, it ended up defining a considerable part of the literature I would seek out in the years that followed.
264: Published in 1939, this Dr. Gideon Fell mystery is known as The Black Spectacles in the United Kingdom, The Problem of the Green Capsule in the United States and Die grüne Kapsel in German.
265: The Problem of the Green Capsule has a very specific importance for me because it was the first book I read entirely in German. I bought it during a trip and have a very strong memory of that moment.
266: The story itself interested me a lot, but, curiously, what made this book so important was the context in which I read it more than the work on its own. It became tied to an experience, a place and a phase of my life. It's one of those cases where the memory around the book becomes almost as important as what's written inside.

Persona 5 Royal came into my life at a very difficult time, and it ended up being much more than just a game I was finishing. It was something that could occupy my mind and put me in that world for a few hours. To this day, one of the things I admire most about it is that feeling of really living in that world, following the days, building relationships and watching the characters change alongside you.

Besides that, the game's design is incredible. The interface, art direction, music and animation give even the simplest things personality. I really like the characters' individual stories and how the game makes you care about that group. And even after finishing it, there's still that urge to go back, try different choices and simply spend more time in that world. It's one of those games that became tied to a specific phase of my life.

307:
Pokémon White represents, for me, Pokémon at its best in several ways at once. Unova is still my favorite Pokédex, and I really like the decision to use an entirely new Pokédex for the main campaign. For the first time in a long while, you genuinely didn't know what you'd find on the next route, and that made the region feel truly new.

I also consider Black & White's story the best Pokémon has ever told. It's one of the few times the franchise tries to directly question the relationship between trainers and Pokémon, and it does so without abandoning the spirit of the series. Visually, I also think it's Pokémon's aesthetic peak: animated sprites, extremely expressive pixel art and a Nintendo DS pushed to its limits. It's probably the game that best represents what I like about Pokémon.

313:
Conker's Bad Fur Day is a game that has no right to be as good as it is. It's absurd, biting, vulgar and completely willing to break expectations, especially considering its era and the console it was released on. But behind all the nonsense is an extremely well thought-out game.

It even became important to my degree because it helped me recognize game design concepts in practice. The game constantly changes its mechanics, plays with different genres and uses its own rules to build jokes and situations. It's disruptive without being disruptive just to get attention. The more I studied game development, the more interesting things I started noticing in it. It's one of the greatest examples of a game being completely ridiculous and extremely intelligent at the same time.

Two teams of eleven try to put the ball into the other team's goal. The goalkeeper, defense, midfield and attack share responsibilities; only the goalkeeper may use their hands, inside their own penalty area. There are two 45-minute halves plus added time.

For offside, position is assessed when a teammate plays the ball: being nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent, in the opposition half, can be an offense if the player becomes actively involved. Fouls can result in free kicks, penalties and cards.
386:
Five on each side. The ball needs to go through the basket, but getting there involves passing, dribbling and movement off the ball. A basket is worth two points, or three from beyond the arc; a free throw is worth one.

Each possession has a time limit for a shot attempt. You can't walk holding the ball without dribbling. Illegal contact can be a foul, leading to an inbound pass or free throws. Period lengths and some details vary by league.
388:
Two teams spend a good while trying to persuade a ball not to land where it should. In practice, they alternate offense and defense over nine innings, normally.

The pitcher throws and the batter tries to hit. The offense scores a run by passing all three bases and returning to home plate. Three outs end a half-inning. Three strikes retire the batter; four balls award first base. Ties may lead to extra innings.

It looks like just accelerating. Then strategy comes in. A weekend usually has practice, qualifying and a race; some also have a sprint, with its own format. Qualifying determines the starting order, subject to penalties.

The race winner is whoever completes the scheduled distance first. Pit stops change tires and strategies. Different compounds balance grip and durability. Weather, traffic, flags and the safety car can turn a race upside down.
